messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sarah sits in the waiting room, her gaze fixed on her own hands, twisting the strap of her purse. At thirty, she feels a century old. It has been six months since the event, and the world has continued to shrink around her until all that remains is the small, suffocating space of her fear. She came to therapy after her husband, Mark, found a credit card statement showing thousands of dollars in debt she had hidden from him, the result of late-night online shopping sprees that offered the only flicker of relief she could find.

The ordeal itself began on a Tuesday evening after she closed her teller window at the bank. The details before the abduction are a blur, but the days that followed are etched into her senses with terrifying clarity. She was held in a basement, a single bare bulb hanging from the ceiling. Her captor rarely spoke, but she was never truly alone. He would sit on a chair in the corner and simply watch her for hours, his presence a heavy, menacing weight in the room. The silence was the worst part; it would stretch on until it was humming with tension, a prelude to the violence she knew was coming. When he finally did speak, his voice was never raised. It was the calm, seething anger in his tone that terrified her most, a quiet promise of pain before the sexual assaults began. That feeling of being observed, a specimen under glass, became the defining feature of her terror.

In the first few weeks after her rescue, Sarah tried to reclaim her life. She went back to her job at the bank, believing routine would be her anchor. But the familiar environment had become a minefield. The gaze of customers waiting in line felt like a physical touch, and she found herself unable to meet their eyes, focusing instead on the counter, her hands, anywhere but their faces. A formal complaint was filed by a customer who found her "unprofessional and distant." The quiet moments between the morning and afternoon rushes, once a time to catch her breath, now felt laden with threat, mirroring the awful, expectant silence of the basement. Her body would go rigid, her heart pounding, certain that something terrible was about to happen. A man expressing mild frustration about a transaction fee was enough to make her flinch, the sound of his voice instantly triggering a wave of panic that left her dizzy and breathless.

At home, things were no better. Mark’s attempts at intimacy, once a source of comfort and connection, were now a trigger for the most vivid and horrifying memories. A simple touch could send her spiraling back to the basement. It wasn't just a thought; it was a complete sensory hijacking. She would feel the cold concrete beneath her, smell the damp, musty air, and see her captor’s face looming over her. The experience was so total, so all-consuming, that she would have to push Mark away and retreat to the bathroom, shaking uncontrollably. She began waking several times a night, her body drenched in a cold sweat, seized by the absolute certainty that she was not safe. She would creep through the house, checking the locks on the doors and windows, her mind not resting until she confirmed she was secure.

To cope, she developed rituals. When the memories threatened to overwhelm her during the day, she would get lost in a mental loop, going over and over the details of the event, trying to make sense of the senseless, as if finding a reason could contain the chaos. At night, when sleep wouldn't come, she would scroll through shopping websites, the thrill of clicking "buy" a temporary balm for her frayed nerves. But the strategies that kept her afloat were also dragging her under. The constant mental review left her exhausted and no closer to an answer. The compulsive spending created a new layer of shame and secrecy. Now, facing the pain in her husband's eyes and the reality of her debt, Sarah is here because she has run out of ways to manage on her own. She feels overwhelmed by the very idea of recalling the event, yet she knows she is a prisoner to it. She is terrified of what revisiting that time will do to her, but even more terrified of a future where she never escapes it.
